title: Morozko
text:
An old man lived with his second wife, her daughter and his own daughter. The stepmother loved her own girl and hated the stepdaughter, who did all the work of the house without complaint. At last the stepmother ordered the old man to take his daughter into the forest in the depth of winter and leave her there. Afraid of his wife, he obeyed, and left his daughter under a fir tree in the snow.

As she sat shivering, Morozko, the Frost, came leaping through the trees, cracking and snapping. "Are you warm, maiden?" he asked. "Warm, Father Frost," she answered gently, though she was freezing. He came lower and the cold grew fiercer, and he asked again. Again she answered kindly. Pleased by her patience and good manners, he wrapped her in furs and blankets and gave her a chest full of rich gifts.

The next day the stepmother sent the old man to bring back the body. He came home with his daughter alive, dressed in finery, with the chest of treasure.

The stepmother at once sent her own daughter out to the same place. When Morozko asked if she was warm, she answered rudely, complaining about the cold and demanding gifts. Morozko froze her stiff. The mother waited for her daughter to come home rich, and the old man brought back only her body.
lesson: Patience and courtesy under hardship tend to be rewarded, and favoritism in a family harms the favored child as well as the neglected one.
people: A stepdaughter, her father, her stepmother, Morozko (Father Frost)
source: Alexander Afanasyev, Russian Folk Tales (Narodnye russkie skazki), Morozko
